title: Runtime Topology Reference
readerIntent: Resolve and audit application, group, environment, server, node, module activation, endpoint, and runtime lifecycle behavior.
priorKnowledge: Understand layered configuration and module metadata.
owner: nConfig hierarchy and lifecycle; environment/server/node modules contribute deployment-specific topology
summary: Runtime topology is derived from package metadata, validated parent ancestry, selected environment/server/node, deterministic indexes, active modules, and layered properties—not naming conventions or handwritten canonical identifiers.

sections.heading: Operator quick checks
items: Resolve environment, server, node, and module identity from current topology metadata before starting or diagnosing a process.
When a server name exists in several environments, supply or interactively select the environment; non-interactive execution must fail clearly rather than guess.
A node requires its server selection. Canonical runtime identity is derived during loading so short human names remain safe across environments.
Verify readiness per composed module, advertised endpoints, direct module communication settings, and optional registration recovery after startup.

sections.heading: Kinds and responsibilities
items: application: project or product boundary; it is not automatically activated as a capability module.
group: organizes modules or environments and may expand configured active lists.
environment: deployable environment root and shared deployment defaults.
server: one runnable process composition and its local activeModules.
node: optional instance-specific child override for coordinates, capacity, worker identity, scheduling, publisher/consumer responsibility, or diagnostics.
module: owned framework, domain, provider, or project capability contributions; kind comes from package.json.nodics, never a folder suffix.

sections.heading: Resolution
items: Resolve startup arguments and candidate packages, validate metadata, select topology, expand groups/parents/required modules, then sort active modules by deterministic dotted index.
The selected physical sequence is environment group, environment/server root, selected server, and selected node when present.
Every concrete child points to the preceding layer through raw parent metadata and sorts parent before child.
Server and node names are local to their parent topology; canonical runtime identity is derived from complete validated ancestry at runtime.
A repeated server name across environments is valid. Interactive ambiguity prompts for environment; non-interactive ambiguity fails with candidates and an explicit command.

sections.heading: Configuration and communication
items: Precedence narrows from environment group to environment/server root, server, and node, after earlier framework/project/module layers.
activeModules activates local schemas, routes, services, pipelines, data, processes, and lifecycle contributions.
servers.* defines local or remote endpoint coordinates and does not activate modules.
Node management observes active router-enabled modules, health, state, and responsibility; it does not choose active modules or own business work.
Internal node/module communication uses governed service identity and secured routes, never human login credentials.

sections.heading: Lifecycle
items: nConfig owns one signal coordinator; modules and providers register bounded lifecycle contributors instead of process signal handlers.
Startup reaches readiness only after required dependencies and mandatory hooks succeed; optional control-plane integrations may recover asynchronously.
SIGTERM or SIGINT marks draining, stops new work, waits boundedly, runs ordered cleanup, and stops.
Hard OOM or SIGKILL requires external restart, replicas, durable ownership, idempotency, and reconciliation because in-process cleanup cannot run.

sections.heading: Verification
items: Test kind and parent validation, duplicate names across environments, deterministic order, interactive and non-interactive ambiguity, node-without-server rejection, activeModules versus servers.* separation, and layered overrides.
Test MonoServer and relevant modular compositions, readiness/degradation, registration recovery, node state, graceful drain, timeouts, provider cleanup, hard-failure reconciliation, and regression.
Do not hardcode environment, server, node, tenant, port, customer-project name, or canonical identity into reusable framework services.

sections.heading: Purpose
paragraphs: This environment proves that the same Nodics capabilities can run either in one backend process or across independently started module runtimes. It contains no BackOffice frontend and does not define a cloud deployment.

sections.heading: Consolidated mode
paragraphs: `monoServer` listens on HTTP port `3000` and activates the configured Nodics module groups in one process. The topology contract verifies Profile, NEMS, Cronjob, Workflow, CMS, WCMS, DEAP data modules, and BackOffice from the effective active-module result rather than assuming that a configured group was loaded successfully. It also verifies that every active module self-registers under one process identity, that the client projection contains no secret or lease-internal fields, and that a complete `monoServer` restart reconstructs the registry while preserving the durable CMS contract selection. The same test performs a real HTTP employee login through Profile and uses that human Bearer token against BackOffice. It proves successful Registry and Bootstrap access plus rejected password, missing-token, insufficient-permission, and service-token-on-human-administration cases.
Run:

```bash
npm run test:topology:consolidated
```

The test uses the configured local bootstrap administrator password for a new local database. If an existing developer database still has an older governed administrator credential, supply it only to the test process:

```bash
NODICS_TOPOLOGY_ADMIN_PASSWORD='<current-local-admin-password>' npm run test:topology:consolidated
```

Do not put that override in `package.json`, committed properties, command history shared with others, or documentation. Rotate legacy local credentials through the Profile identity-governance process; startup must not overwrite a human password merely to make a test pass. Without the override, a legacy credential mismatch is reported as `SKIPPED_LEGACY_LOCAL_CREDENTIAL`; all non-login topology checks still run. Acceptance evidence for the human journey requires a run that reports the six HTTP outcomes, not the skipped status.

sections.heading: Modular mode
paragraphs:
| Runtime | HTTP port | Required capability |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `profileServer` | 3000 | Profile identity and tenant authority |
| `deapServer` | 3010 | Data Consumer, Processor, and Publisher |
| `nemsServer` | 3020 | NEMS event capability |
| `cronServer` | 3030 | Cronjob scheduling capability |
| `cmsStagedServer` | 3040 | Versioned CMS authoring, WCMS, Workflow, and nPublish |
| `workflowServer` | 3050 | Independently deployable Workflow capability |
| `backofficeServer` | 3060 | BackOffice registry and discovery |
| `cmsOnlineServer` | 3070 | Non-versioned CMS delivery target |
Run:

```bash
npm run test:topology:modular
```
For manual startup, select the environment explicitly because short server names may also exist under Dev, QA, PreProd, or Prod:

```bash
ENV=startioLocal SERVER=profileServer node -e 'require("./nodics").start()'
ENV=startioLocal SERVER=cronServer NODE=cronNode0 node -e 'require("./nodics").start()'
```
In an interactive terminal, `SERVER=cronServer` offers matching environments. Non-interactive execution requires `ENV` and fails rather than guessing.

The modular contract starts all listed processes, verifies their effective module composition and readiness, exercises direct module communication, checks BackOffice self-registration and recovery, and proves Staged-to-Online publication behavior. CMS Staged and CMS Online register as distinct runtime instances with different direct-call endpoints while the catalogue aggregates them under one CMS capability. A module or BackOffice restart must reconcile without blocking unrelated runtime traffic.

The distributed security journey logs in through `profileServer` and calls `backofficeServer` with the resulting human Bearer token. It repeats after a Profile restart and after a BackOffice restart, proving tenant preservation and the same 401/403 rejection boundaries as consolidated mode. Profile restart replaces only its runtime identity; unrelated registered identities remain.

The registry-derived direct-call journey selects and pings eight advertised module endpoints: Profile, NEMS, Cronjob, Data Consumer, dedicated Workflow, CMS Staged, CMS Online, and BackOffice. CMS selection without a server role is rejected as ambiguous. Data Processor and Data Publisher are registered without endpoints because they are internal DEAP composition, not client-callable APIs. This prevents the registry from inventing a parallel router or exposing modules that do not own an HTTP boundary.

sections.heading: CMS Staged and Online boundary
paragraphs: The two CMS runtimes are separate systems, not aliases for one database. `startioCmsStaged` contains versioned authoring data and approval state; `startioCmsOnline` contains non-versioned published delivery state. Staged uses the existing named module connections to publish approved CMS, Pricing, and Product manifests. Online must never read the Staged database as a fallback.

sections.heading: Configuration and customization
paragraphs: The authoritative local topology declaration is `startio/envs/startioLocal/config/properties.js#test.runtimeTopology`. A project environment may override the server list, required effective modules, and communication checks through normal Nodics property layering. Do not add a second launcher or hardcoded test-only module registry.

Server ports, active modules, databases, connections, and runtime roles remain owned by the corresponding server module `config/properties.js` files. Change the smallest environment or server property necessary; do not copy framework lifecycle, authentication, event, publication, or registry services.
